title: Gou Jian Tastes the Gall
text:
In 494 BC King Gou Jian of Yue was crushed by King Fu Chai of Wu and trapped with his last troops on Mount Kuaiji. On the advice of his ministers he surrendered, and according to tradition he and his wife went to Wu to serve its king in humiliation before being allowed to return home. Sima Qian himself says little about this captivity.

Back in Yue, Gou Jian did not forget. Sima Qian writes that he hung a gall bladder where he sat and tasted its bitterness before eating or lying down, asking himself whether he had forgotten the shame of Kuaiji. He worked in the fields with his own hands, his wife wove her own cloth, he ate simple food, and he treated the people and talented men generously. With his ministers Fan Li and Wen Zhong he spent years building up the population, the economy and the army, while sending gifts to Wu and appearing loyal.

Fu Chai, meanwhile, turned to wars with northern states and ignored warnings about Yue. When Wu's army was far away, Yue struck. After years of further fighting, in 473 BC Yue besieged the Wu capital. Fu Chai asked for terms, as Gou Jian once had, but was refused, and he killed himself. The later idiom "sleeping on brushwood and tasting gall" became the Chinese expression for enduring hardship to prepare a comeback.
lesson: A defeat need not be the end if you keep the memory sharp and use the years well. Patient, quiet rebuilding can reverse a loss.
people: Gou Jian of Yue, Fu Chai of Wu, Fan Li, Wen Zhong
location: Yue and Wu (modern Zhejiang and Jiangsu, China)
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapter 41
caveat: The detail of sleeping on brushwood was added in later retellings; Sima Qian mentions only the gall.
